item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This is a solid take on the old Bermuda Triangle Flight 19 archetype, but I think it slips up in two areas. Other than the temporal distortion, it's not much different than those Triangle archetypes, so it doesn't perplex or unnerve with anything unfamiliar. And the final unredacted contact log, where we hear the crew screaming, dissipates rather than elevates the tension.

As the reader proceeds through -998, they wonder what happened to the aircraft and its crew - whether it has entered another dimension or been abducted by very slothful aliens. but the terror here comes from the timestamps and the sense of being lost; -998 operates on the fear of displacement, a state which cannot be localized or identified. Screams, on the other hand, are a sign of acute terror, an immediate threat — something on the wing, a mountain looming from the fog, gas in the cabin, Barry Manilow on the intercom, whatever. This kills the building tension; it asks the reader to shift gears from 'my God, this crew is lost for years and will never come home' to 'my God, this crew is terrified of something right there'. That's effective in some ways, but it doesn't make good use of the prior material, and thinking about a monster in the cabin, or enormous tentacles in the fog, isn't as terrifying or uncertain as thinking about being lost forever in an alien place.

Long story short, I'd like permission from the original author to remove that log entry and try to brainstorm something new in its place, something that deploys the same kind of tension the rest of -998 has been building up - isolation, disorientation, distance, fears of being lost forever - rather than a jump scare. I'm not totally sure what yet, but I bet we can come up with something cool.

One additional thought I had was the idea of adding a note about increasing redshift on signals from the lost aircraft, which could indirectly suggest it was being drawn away in some inexorable and inexplicable fashion. This is a technical detail which adds verisimilitude and a bit of creep factor without smashing the reader over the head. It could also be read as an effect of whatever temporal state the aircraft is trapped in.
